idiom_name: protocol as the policy contract, generic parameter as the binding
implementation_notes: Swift's realization is a host generic over a protocol-constrained policy (struct Cache<Element, Policy: EvictionPolicy> where Policy.Element == Element): the protocol states the contract, conformance is checked at the call site, and specialization gives static dispatch on hot paths; `some EvictionPolicy` in a parameter position is the same binding written shorter. Protocol extensions - optionally where-constrained - provide default implementations and conditional enrichment (extension Cache where Policy: Introspectable { ... }), replacing the inheritance-based enrichment of the classic form, while `any EvictionPolicy` (an existential) is the run-time alternative when the policy must vary after creation. Prefer the generic form on hot paths: existentials box values and dispatch through a witness table.
pitfalls: A protocol with an associated type cannot be used as a bare type: reaching for `any EvictionPolicy` reintroduces witness-table dispatch and boxing, losing the generic binding's specialization.
Storing the policy as `any EvictionPolicy` in the host also erases the associated Element type, forcing casts or additional type-erasing wrappers at every policy call.
Protocol extensions can add default methods but no stored state, so stateful policies must be concrete types or classes - and class policies are reference-shared between hosts.
